title: Python Foundations
description: Write and run the Python the rest of the course is built on.

lessons.title: Types, formatting, and control flow
lessons.lead: Two short programs: one about types and f-strings, one about branching inside a loop.

tasks.title: Describe a student
tasks.brief: Print the type of `score`, then the same value as a whole number, then one formatted sentence.
steps: Use `type(score)` for the first line
Use `int(score)` for the second  it truncates rather than rounds
Use an f-string for the third line
tasks.hint: An f-string can hold any expression: `f"{name} scored {score}"`.
tasks.explain: `int()` drops the decimal part rather than rounding  `int(87.5)` is 87, not 88.

tasks.title: Grade every score
tasks.brief: Loop over the scores and print each one followed by its letter grade.
steps: 90 and above is an A, 80 and above is a B, anything else is a C
Print the score and the letter on one line, separated by a space
starter: # decide the grade, then print it
tasks.hint: Check the highest boundary first  an `elif` only runs when the branch above it did not.
tasks.explain: Order matters. If you tested `>= 80` first, a 95 would be caught by it and never reach the A branch.

lessons.title: Parameters, defaults, and return values
lessons.lead: Package logic behind a name so it can be reused and tested.

tasks.title: Two small functions
tasks.brief: Write `celsius_to_fahrenheit(c)` and `is_passing(score, passing=50)`, then print the four calls already in the starter.
steps: The conversion is `c * 9 / 5 + 32`
`is_passing` returns True or False, and the pass mark defaults to 50
tasks.hint: Both functions need `return`, not `print`  the printing is already written for you.
tasks.explain: `score >= passing` already evaluates to True or False  an `if` that returns True or False around it would just be longer.

tasks.title: Summarise a list of scores
tasks.brief: Write `summarise(scores)` returning a dictionary with the count, min, max, and average rounded to two places.
steps: Use the keys `count`, `min`, `max`, and `avg` in that order
Round the average with `round(value, 2)`
Return `{}` when the list is empty, so the function never divides by zero
tasks.hint: `sum()`, `len()`, `min()`, and `max()` all take the list directly.
tasks.explain: Guarding the empty case first  a guard clause  keeps the main body free of nesting.

lessons.title: Order versus lookup
lessons.lead: The two containers you will use every day, ending with the shape most raw data arrives in.

tasks.title: Slice, add, and sort
tasks.brief: Print the first score, the last score, the middle two as a list, and then every score sorted from highest to lowest.
steps: Index from the back with `[-1]`
The middle two are positions 1 and 2
Add 95 to the list before sorting
starter: # append 95, then print the list sorted highest first
tasks.hint: `sorted(scores, reverse=True)` returns a new list and leaves the original alone.
tasks.explain: `scores[1:3]` stops before position 3, so it gives two items, not three.

tasks.title: A table as a list of dictionaries
tasks.brief: From the list of student dictionaries, print the names of everyone who passed, then the class average to one decimal place.
steps: The pass mark is 50
Collect the passing names into a list and print that list
Format the average as `class average: 67.3`
starter: # names of the students who passed
tasks.hint: `f"{value:.1f}"` formats a number to one decimal place.
solution: average = sum(s["score"] for s in students) / len(students)
tasks.explain: One dictionary is one row, and the list of them is the table. This is the shape a Pandas DataFrame wraps in Module 04.

lessons.title: Reading and writing real data
lessons.lead: These run against a small in-memory file system, so the files you write here are real files as far as your code is concerned.

tasks.title: Write a file, then read it back
tasks.brief: Write three lines to `notes.txt`, then read the file back and print each line with its number.
steps: Open with `"w"` to write, then again with `"r"` to read
Pass `encoding="utf-8"` both times
Strip the trailing newline before printing
Number the lines starting at 1
starter: lines = ["load the data", "clean the data", "plot the data"]
# 2. read it back and print: 1 load the data
tasks.hint: `f.write()` does not add a newline for you  append `\n` yourself.
solution: lines = ["load the data", "clean the data", "plot the data"]
for number, line in enumerate(f, start=1):
tasks.explain: `enumerate(f, start=1)` counts as it loops, and looping over the file object reads it one line at a time  the right approach for a file too large to hold in memory.

Everything `DictReader` produces is a string
Use `max(rows, key=...)` to find the top row
